rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tempestuous wind that covers the earth with pebbles and sand is a pebble-hurling wind.
rows.anchor: Analogously, the tempestuous wind which covers the earth with pebbles and sand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s people were struck first by stones in a dust-laden wind, then by a wind strong enough to overturn buildings; Islahi cites 29:40 and 15:74.
rows.anchor: The Almighty unleashed on the people of Lot a dust-laden wind which after picking up speed became a pebble-hurling wind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording depicts a situation beyond words, implying that the people were covered by something indescribable.
rows.anchor: It is used to portray a situation which is beyond words. The implication is that it was covered with something which is beyond words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the pronoun is singular, Quraysh as a whole is addressed so that every individual is warned.
rows.anchor: Though the pronoun is in the singular,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The evidence for reward and punishment comes from reason, revelation, the scriptures of Moses and Abraham, and the histories of their nations.
rows.anchor: These arguments which substantiate reward and punishment are before them.

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally interpret al-ālāʾ as favours and blessings, a gloss Islahi calls incomplete.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have generally interpreted it to mean “favours and blessings;”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ālāʾ includes miracles, signs, natural marvels, feats, relics, and signs of wisdom; blessings fall within this broader meaning, but are not always an adequate translation.
rows.anchor: Its real meaning is miracles, signs, marvels of nature, feats, relics and signs of wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi points to the word’s many nuances in Sūrah al-Raḥmān and to Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī’s research in Mufradāt al-Qur’ān.
rows.anchor: My mentor, Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī has presented his scholarly research on this word in his Mufradāt al-Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion returns to the opening: the Qur’an is divine revelation and a warner like earlier messengers; its promised hour is near and inescapable, so its hearers should grieve, wake, prostrate to God, and worship Him alone.
rows.anchor: the same subject with which the sūrah began is brought up as a reminder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative pronoun at the start of the closing passage refers to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: refers to the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the Prophet, but that changes little because his message and the Qur’an are one; 65:10 distinguishes the Qur’an as dhikr and the Prophet as rasūl while treating them as one entity.
rows.anchor: both are in the capacity of a single entity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nudhūr is the plural of nadhīr and refers to all earlier prophets and scriptures.
rows.anchor: refers to all the previous prophets and scriptures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is not a joke: those who mock it will face consequences like the earlier nations.
rows.anchor: if they make fun of it, they should remember that they will face its consequences in the very manner the previous nations faced them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-āzifah means what has drawn near and refers to the looming divine punishment; it must not be considered far off.
rows.anchor: refers to the divine punishment of which the Qur’ān was warning these people: they should not consider it to be far off; it is now looming over their heads.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s practice is to give a warned nation respite only until the truth is conclusively conveyed, then destroy it if it persists in denial; this punishment anticipates the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: As soon as this period expires, that nation is destroyed if it persists in its denial of the messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that none but God can avert the punishment means that Lāt, Manāt, ‘Uzzā, and other deities cannot save them.
rows.anchor: except for God no one will be able to get rid of it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their amazement at a Book warning of a great punishment is misplaced: it calls for anxiety and tears, yet they laugh.
rows.anchor: it is something to cry about and be very anxious of; however, instead of crying, they are laughing at it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samidūn means unconscious or senseless: while the Book tries to shake them, they remain in an indifferent slumber.
rows.anchor: The verse says that this Book is trying to shake and jolt them, while they are overcome with the slumber of indifference.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To escape danger, they must wake from indifference, forsake other deities, and prostrate and worship God alone; no one else can save them from the calamity.
rows.anchor: only prostrate themselves before God and serve and worship Him only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah begins with stars falling and setting and ends with prostration and worship of God alone.
rows.anchor: This sūrah began with the falling and setting of stars and it ends on prostration and worship to God alone.

none: Bare sūrah title page with no commentary to record.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to dissociate concerns those who fought the Muslims and forced them and the Prophet to leave; people who did not do so should be treated justly and virtuously.
rows.anchor: those who have not done so, should be dealt with justice and in a virtuous way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Women migrating from Mecca should be examined for faith and accepted only if they migrated specifically for Islam.
rows.anchor: If it is proven that they have migrated specifically for the cause of Islam, only then should they be included in the ranks of the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims may not remain married to idolatrous women; they should release them and exchange the dowers.
rows.anchor: It is not lawful for the Muslims to keep idolatrous women in marriage. They should liberate them and mutually exchange the dowers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to take a pledge from women who come to Islam and intend to live by its directives.
rows.anchor: take a pledge from women who come to him for the cause of Islam and intend to lead their lives purely according to its directives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the sūrah’s end Muslims are warned against befriending Jews and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: At the very end of the sūrah, Muslims are warned not to establish friendship with the Jews and the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews and disbelievers will meet the same fate, having been shaken from their roots.
rows.anchor: Both shall meet the same fate: they have been shaken from their very roots.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although verse 60:1 addresses Muslims generally, it specifically targets those who continued relations with the enemy after migration.
rows.anchor: even after passing through the phase of migration, still held relations with
